newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan factions plan rival HK handover rallies.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan factions plan rival HK handover rallies.

text.p: Democratic but diplomatically isolated Taiwan is to stage two rival rallies marking Hong Kong's return to China, highlighting deep divisions among the island's 21 million people over their own future.
Pro-independence activists were making final preparations on Thursday for Saturday's long-planned "Say No to China, Say Yes to Taiwan" rally, predicting tens of thousands would take part.

Not to be outdone, a Chinese nationalist group announced plans on Thursday for their own big rally on Sunday to celebrate Hong Kong's return to China -- though they stopped short of dubbing the event "Say Yes to China".
"Hong Kong's return symbolises the end of colonialism in China," Shih Wei-chen, secretary-general of Taiwan's Chinese Nation United Front, told Reuters by telephone.
"It should be celebrated by all Chinese people," she said.
The front unites several "patriotic" groups that advocate ending the separation of Taiwan, Hong Kong and Portuguese-run Macau from China, Shih said.

"We believe the Chinese nation should reunify," Shih said. "We are not a political party so we will not suggest how China should be reunified. All Chinese people should work out a resolution for the reunification."
Pro-independence groups vowed to send a bold message to China and the world that Taiwan strongly rejects the "one country, two systems" formula being pioneered in Hong Kong.

"The international community may recognise one China as (being) legitimately represented by the Beijing government, but it may not force Taiwan to become a part of China," protest organisers said in a statement.

Beijing has viewed Taiwan as a rebel-held province since a civil war split them in 1949, pressing ever harder to force the island's exiled Republic of China government out of existence so Taiwan can be reabsorbed under Beijing's sovereignty.

Taipei officially favours eventual reunification, but flatly rejects the "one country, two systems" offer of local autonomy under Beijing's rule, arguing that the communists have never fully dislodged the exiled republic's sovereignty.
Taiwan, which has embraced multiparty democracy, maintains that union is impossible before the Communist Party allows a political liberalisation that ends its monopoly on power.
The pro-independence activists said Taiwan already was a sovereign nation and could not take Hong Kong as a model.
"Before July 1, the people on Taiwan will clearly express their determination to go in a direction opposite that of Hong Kong in various activities," it said.
Beijing says the long-negotiated return of Hong Kong and Macau in 1999 will leave Taiwan as the only territory still awaiting "reunification with the motherland".
China says its handling of Hong Kong's "one country, two systems" experience should reassure Taiwan of its own future with the mainland.
Under the system agreed by Britain and China in 1984, Hong Kong can maintain its capitalist systems for 50 years.
Beijing has pledged that Taiwan would have even greater autonomy if it accepted "one country, two systems".
Taiwan independence groups will have none of it. Activists vowed to apply for U.N. membership as the Republic of Taiwan -- a move that is certain to anger Beijing.
Beijing has repeatedly said it would attack Taiwan if it opts for independence.
